title: Interaction craft: four practitioners, concrete decisions
scope: Public-source learning notes. Selection is a study set, not a verified award result or ranking.
method: Read primary essays and canonical project documentation. Source links were opened successfully. Descriptions of demos come from their authors; interactions and performance were not independently tested. Decisions distinguish documented choices from our interpretation of their costs.

people.name: Rauno Freiberg
people.focus: Interaction reasoning, restrained motion, and visual implementation

artifacts.title: Invisible Details of Interaction Design
artifacts.author: Rauno Freiberg
artifacts.sourceType: Primary essay with personal prototypes and analysis of others' products
artifacts.confidence: High for his reported experiments; observational for explanations of Apple behavior
artifacts.summary: Studies gesture commitment, interruption, spatial consistency, and repetition. His bookmarking-tool example shows that removing motion can improve perceived speed.

artifacts.title: Crafting the Next.js Website
artifacts.author: Rauno Freiberg; website collaboration with Glenn (@glennui) and @almonk, with the design credited to Glenn
artifacts.sourceType: Primary implementation case study with code
artifacts.confidence: High; authorship boundaries are explicit in the introduction
artifacts.summary: Explains how a team shipped the static improvement first, then refined animation, focus states, and rendering details.

artifacts.title: Designing Depth
artifacts.author: Rauno Freiberg
artifacts.sourceType: Primary visual essay and Vercel marketing iteration
artifacts.confidence: High for his described iteration; Apple's intentions are explicitly hypothesized
artifacts.summary: Connects layered photographic composition to software hierarchy, then decomposes interface motion into ordered states.

decisions.decision: Remove animation from the bookmarking tool's frequently repeated keyboard operations.
decisions.alternative: Keep the animated active indicator and list mutations, merely shortening their timing.
decisions.tradeoff: The documented result is greater perceived speed. Our interpretation: sacrifice an attractive demonstration to reduce friction during sustained use.
decisions.attribution: Personal implementation decision reported by Rauno

decisions.decision: Animate the opacity of pre-styled shadow layers in the Next.js switchboard.
decisions.tradeoff: Avoids repeated painting described in the case study. Our interpretation: extra pseudo-element structure purchases more predictable motion on weaker devices.
decisions.attribution: Rauno's implementation within a credited team project

decisions.decision: Ship the improved static Next.js site before all animation refinements.
decisions.alternative: Hold the entire redesign in an increasingly large pull request.
decisions.tradeoff: The team delivered a useful intermediate state. Our interpretation: staged quality requires follow-through, but avoids making polish a prerequisite for any improvement.
decisions.attribution: Team decision described by Rauno, not sole authorship

decisions.decision: Build depth in the Preview Deployments visual using blurred background, softened boundaries, and additional browser frames.
decisions.alternative: Keep flat overlapping panels or add unrelated decorative objects.
decisions.tradeoff: The added layers communicate the product's abundance of deployments. Our interpretation: visual richness earns its place when it reinforces the subject rather than competing with it.
decisions.attribution: Rauno's described iteration on a Vercel marketing visual

writingTechniques.technique: Turn an impression into a discriminating question
writingTechniques.evidence: The swipe section asks when an action should commit, then contrasts reversible exploration with destructive dismissal. The explanation depends on intent, not a blanket rule about fluidity.
The depth essay shows a weak composition and successive revisions before discussing choreography. Readers can connect a particular edit to a particular improvement.

writingTechniques.technique: Disclose inference rather than impersonating the original designer
writingTechniques.evidence: The choreography discussion marks the suggested reason for delaying the keyboard as an assumption. Observable sequencing and proposed intent remain separate.

exercise.task: Choose one keyboard-heavy flow and one direct-manipulation flow. Prototype each with and without motion, then use each repeatedly rather than judging a single playback.
exercise.deliverable: Four short recordings and a decision note stating what motion communicates, where interruption works, and what was removed.
exercise.evaluation: Can you recover from a mistaken action immediately? Does motion explain a relationship? Does the fiftieth repetition still help?

limitations: These are three works, not a comprehensive assessment of his output.
Apple examples are analysis, not evidence that Rauno designed those interactions.
Browser-specific implementation advice from 2023 needs current compatibility testing.
The essays report craft judgments rather than controlled usability measurements.
people.coverage: Three primary works read; publication months visible. High confidence in documented decisions and attribution. No source repository audit or hands-on demo testing.

people.name: Emil Kowalski
people.focus: Interruptible motion, gesture edge cases, and teachable component craft

artifacts.title: 7 Practical Animation Tips
artifacts.dateNote: No publication date visible in the inspected page; reviewed 2026-11-05.
artifacts.author: Emil Kowalski
artifacts.sourceType: Primary instructional essay with paired interactive examples
artifacts.confidence: High for recommendations; their effectiveness is not independently measured here
artifacts.summary: Makes responsiveness concrete through easing comparisons, origin-aware scaling, tooltip timing, and repetition-sensitive animation choices.

artifacts.title: Building a toast component
artifacts.dateNote: Article recalls building Sonner in 2023; that is not established as this page's publication date.
artifacts.author: Emil Kowalski
artifacts.confidence: High; personal first-person account, not a repository audit
artifacts.summary: Connects retargetable animation to toast stacking, then covers a simple calling API and details such as pausing dismissal while the tab is hidden.

artifacts.title: Building a drawer component
artifacts.dateNote: No publication date visible in the inspected page; reviewed 2026-11-05.
artifacts.author: Emil Kowalski
artifacts.confidence: High for described design process; historical implementation notes
artifacts.summary: Builds on Radix Dialog, then works through dragging, scrolling, virtual keyboards, multiple touches, and snap points.

decisions.decision: Use retargetable CSS transitions for toasts whose positions change during rapid arrivals.
decisions.alternative: Keep the initial CSS keyframe implementation.
decisions.tradeoff: Existing toasts can transition toward new destinations instead of jumping. Our interpretation: an interaction that can be interrupted needs a state model, not only a polished entrance.

decisions.decision: Update the drawer element's transform directly during dragging.
decisions.alternative: Update an inherited CSS variable used for the transform.
decisions.tradeoff: His investigation traced lag in larger drawers to descendant style recalculation. The choice localizes hot-path updates; it does not imply CSS variables are generally slow.

decisions.decision: Allow drawer dragging only at the content's scroll boundary, with a short lockout after returning to the top.
decisions.alternative: Immediately turn a fast upward scroll into a momentum-based dismissal gesture.
decisions.tradeoff: The reported 100 ms guard prevents accidental closure. Our interpretation: a small delay protects intent at the boundary between two gesture meanings.

decisions.decision: Delay the first tooltip, but show subsequent tooltips in the group immediately without animation.
decisions.alternative: Apply the same entrance delay and motion to every tooltip.
decisions.tradeoff: Initial delay discourages accidental activation; subsequent immediacy supports intentional scanning. This is a contextual timing rule, not a call to make every tooltip instantaneous.
decisions.attribution: Emil's recommendation, with behavior credited to existing component libraries

writingTechniques.technique: Hold a variable constant in a comparison
writingTechniques.evidence: The easing demonstration keeps duration at 300 ms while comparing curves. This teaches readers to isolate perceived responsiveness from elapsed time.
The toast essay asks readers to add toasts quickly before presenting the replacement animation approach. The flaw becomes visible before the explanation.
The drawer narrative explains why eliminating React rerenders did not eliminate lag, then identifies inherited-style recalculation as the missing cause.

exercise.task: Build a three-toast stack and deliberately send ten notifications rapidly. Compare an entrance-only implementation with retargetable transitions; also test long content and backgrounding the tab.
exercise.deliverable: Two recordings, a tiny state diagram, and a table of interruption, dismissal, visibility, and reduced-motion behavior.
exercise.evaluation: No positional jumps, unread notifications are not silently lost, and removing motion still leaves clear status.

limitations: The animation tips' sub-300 ms guideline is not universal: the drawer case describes 500 ms motion for a different context.
Vaul's keyboard workaround admits a delayed viewport adjustment; native imitation carries real browser costs.
Emil credits Radix foundations and react-hot-toast API inspiration. These are not claims of inventing all underlying patterns.
No article publication dates were inferred from project launch dates.
people.coverage: Three primary works read. High confidence in reported choices; unknown publication dates. Performance and accessibility were not independently tested.

people.name: shadcn
people.focus: Editable defaults, component ownership, and code distribution as product design

artifacts.title: shadcn/ui Introduction
artifacts.author: shadcn/ui project; page has no individual byline
artifacts.confidence: High for project principles; moderate for individual authorship
artifacts.summary: Defines owned, editable component code, shared composition, and useful defaults as the product's organizing principles.

artifacts.title: Theming
artifacts.author: shadcn/ui project; page has no individual byline
artifacts.summary: Uses semantic surface/foreground token pairs so global themes can change without rewriting component classes.

artifacts.title: Registry: Getting Started
artifacts.author: shadcn/ui project; page has no individual byline
artifacts.confidence: High for documented workflow; not executed in this study
artifacts.summary: Builds a registry from a small component, then covers composition, serving, discovery, installation, and publication.

artifacts.title: registry-item.json specification
artifacts.author: shadcn/ui project; page has no individual byline
artifacts.confidence: High for schema contracts; not pinned to a repository commit
artifacts.summary: Makes package dependencies, registry dependencies, file types, and destination paths explicit distribution data.

decisions.decision: Deliver editable component source as the customization boundary.
decisions.alternative: Require all customization through an installed package's public API, wrappers, and style overrides.
decisions.tradeoff: The project explicitly prioritizes local control. Our interpretation: teams gain freedom but must own divergence, review, and incorporation of later upstream fixes.
decisions.attribution: Documented project principle, not a verified sole-author decision

decisions.decision: Use semantic color roles with paired foreground tokens.
decisions.alternative: Encode literal color choices independently inside each component.
decisions.tradeoff: Theme changes become centralized. Our interpretation: token names make intent legible, but a coherent token vocabulary and contrast testing remain the adopting team's responsibility.

decisions.decision: Describe source distribution with explicit files, dependencies, and configurable destinations.
decisions.alternative: Ask adopters to copy snippets and reconstruct hidden setup requirements manually.
decisions.tradeoff: The schema makes installation repeatable across project layouts. Our interpretation: metadata becomes part of the product and must be maintained as carefully as component code.

decisions.decision: Let larger registries compose multiple source manifests, then resolve them into a consumable catalog.
decisions.alternative: Require one manually maintained, monolithic manifest.
decisions.tradeoff: The guide supports local organization without pushing that complexity onto consumers. Our interpretation: authors must still understand relative paths and the distinction between authoring structure and distribution output.
decisions.attribution: Documented current project architecture, not claimed as original launch behavior

writingTechniques.technique: Explain the category through a concrete frustration
writingTechniques.evidence: The introduction starts with conventional package use, then describes customization workarounds before introducing editable code. The architecture answers a recognizable problem.
The theming page pairs role definitions with tiny token and utility examples, then maps roles to real component uses.
The registry guide does not end at a successful build: it walks through listing, searching, inspecting, and installing what was produced.

exercise.task: Create one editable status component with semantic light/dark tokens and an explicit dependency manifest. Adapt it to two visibly different brands, then simulate an upstream accessibility fix.
exercise.deliverable: Two variants, a source diff, a registry item draft, and a one-paragraph update policy.
exercise.evaluation: Can another developer understand ownership, change the theme without searching every class, and merge the fix without losing local behavior?

limitations: This is project-level evidence. Current documentation does not establish that shadcn personally wrote every page or made every later decision.
Editable code does not automatically guarantee accessibility after customization.
The study did not measure adoption, maintenance cost, or performance, and does not use popularity as proof of quality.
The current registry docs may differ substantially from the original release; no launch chronology is claimed.
people.coverage: Four canonical documentation artifacts read, plus repository README for provenance. Strong architectural evidence; weaker personal authorship evidence. Live docs are not commit-pinned.

additionalSources.title: shadcn/ui source repository
additionalSources.note: README and project provenance inspected; source implementation not audited.

additionalSources.title: Registry introduction
additionalSources.note: Confirms distribution scope extends beyond React components.

people.name: Devon Govett
people.focus: Inclusive interaction architecture and explaining the hidden complexity of UI primitives

artifacts.title: Taming the dragon: Accessible drag and drop
artifacts.author: Devon Govett; describes React Aria/React Spectrum team work
artifacts.confidence: High for authorship and reported architecture
artifacts.summary: Combines native drag interoperability with keyboard and screen-reader interaction, then explains why a higher-level API was added.

artifacts.title: Date and Time Pickers for All
artifacts.author: Devon Govett; explicitly credits Adobe design, accessibility, internationalization, and product teams
artifacts.sourceType: Bylined primary design and engineering case study
artifacts.summary: Shows how locale ambiguity changes input design, and separates date-entry tasks from calendar-browsing tasks.

artifacts.title: Building a Button Part 1: Press Events
artifacts.author: Devon Govett; React Spectrum/Aria/Stately team work
artifacts.confidence: High for the historical rationale; browser-specific details require current validation
artifacts.summary: Derives a unified press abstraction from touch cancellation, duplicate events, keyboard repetition, and virtual screen-reader activation.

artifacts.title: Scrolling is All You Need: Building a Swipeable Sheet
artifacts.author: Devon Govett; credits Nikolas Schröter for usePreventScroll improvements
artifacts.sourceType: Bylined primary component architecture case study
artifacts.confidence: High for reported design; cross-browser behavior not independently tested
artifacts.summary: Uses native scrolling, snap points, and view timelines for sheet gestures, with explicit handling of nested content and software keyboards.

decisions.decision: Retain native HTML drag-and-drop interoperability while adding accessible interaction modes.
decisions.alternative: Use a self-contained custom drag system or provide only a separate copy/paste workaround.
decisions.tradeoff: Native inter-app and file transfer remains possible despite browser quirks. Keyboard drag mode limits navigation to valid targets. Our interpretation: parity is treated as core architecture, not a later escape hatch.

decisions.decision: Use individually labeled date segments rather than parsing an unrestricted text field.
decisions.alternative: Accept ambiguous free-form date strings and try to infer the user's format.
decisions.tradeoff: Locale determines field order, and mobile users get numeric entry. Our interpretation: constrained entry gives up free-form expressiveness in exchange for less ambiguity and clearer screen-reader context.
decisions.attribution: Explicit multi-team design decision described by Devon

decisions.decision: Expose a unified press lifecycle rather than treating click as the whole interaction.
decisions.alternative: Independently wire pointer, keyboard, and click handlers in every component.
decisions.tradeoff: Normalization avoids duplicate activation and preserves cancellation, including virtual clicks from assistive technology. Our interpretation: complexity moves into a reusable primitive instead of disappearing.
decisions.attribution: React Aria team implementation explained by Devon
decisions.sourceSection: Virtual press events; Unified press events

decisions.decision: Drive the sheet with native overflow scrolling, scroll snapping, and view-timeline animation.
decisions.alternative: Implement every touch movement and momentum calculation in JavaScript.
decisions.tradeoff: The article reports off-main-thread gestures and native physics. Our interpretation: platform primitives replace custom gesture code, but introduce non-obvious geometry, nested-scroll policy, and compatibility requirements.
decisions.attribution: React Aria team architecture explained by Devon
decisions.sourceSection: Setting up the viewport; Gesture-synced animations

writingTechniques.technique: Start with the apparently trivial object, then reveal its test matrix
writingTechniques.evidence: The button essay moves from a native element to mouse, touch, keyboard, and virtual activation, using concrete failure sequences to justify abstraction.

writingTechniques.technique: Use an ambiguous example to establish the requirement
writingTechniques.evidence: A numeric date that can mean either February or March makes locale parsing uncertainty tangible before the segmented-field solution is introduced.
The sheet article exposes timeline progress, opacity, radius, and the clipped scroller area in its teaching demo. The reader can connect the illusion to its mechanism.

exercise.task: Design a two-list transfer interaction for mouse, keyboard, and screen reader use. Write the valid-target and cancellation rules before styling it.
exercise.deliverable: A state diagram, an announcement script, and recordings of all three input paths, including an invalid drop and a canceled operation.
exercise.evaluation: Every path must accomplish the same task, preserve predictable focus, explain the available destination, and avoid accidental duplicate actions.

limitations: Bylined explanations are Devon's writing; the component systems are collaborative work.
The 2020 and 2022 posts are historical accounts, not current browser-support matrices.
A library's accessibility claims still need testing in the consuming product and with actual users.
The sheet article does not establish a universal performance win over Vaul or every JavaScript approach; no comparative benchmark was run.
people.coverage: Four bylined primary works read, all with visible dates. High confidence in documented rationale and team attribution. No assistive-technology test or repository audit performed.

crossStudy.title: Time is part of an interaction's meaning
crossStudy.lesson: Compare Rauno's removed keyboard animation with Emil's immediate subsequent tooltips. Ask whether a delay serves intent in this exact repeated action rather than treating motion as a universal quality signal.

crossStudy.title: A newer platform can change the implementation answer
crossStudy.lesson: Study Emil's Vaul gesture/scroll arbitration beside React Aria's October 2026 native-scroll sheet. Their common problem is clear; the available browser mechanisms and historical constraints differ. This is a comparison of reasoning, not a winner declaration.

crossStudy.title: Design an adoption path, not only a component
crossStudy.lesson: shadcn's registry guide tests discovery through installation; Devon's drag-and-drop account describes adding high-level operations when the low-level API required too much boilerplate. Both make the easiest useful path a design concern.
